response:
Your design has two grouping factors — participants and sentences (items) — and they are crossed, not nested: every participant read every sentence. That structure demands a crossed random-effects model, not a simple by-subject random-intercept model.

Step 1: Map the data structure
- Unit of observation: one reading time per participant × sentence combination (40 × 80 = 3,200 rows).
- Grouping factors: participants (N = 40) and items/sentences (N = 80). Because every participant saw every sentence, these are fully crossed — there is no hierarchy between them.
- Fixed predictor: ambiguity (ambiguous vs. unambiguous). This manipulation varies within participants (each person saw both types) but is between items (each sentence is inherently ambiguous or not).

Step 2: Random-effects structure

Following the maximal-model principle (Barr, Levy, Scheepers & Tily, 2013 — "Keep It Maximal"), the random-effects structure should include everything the design supports:
- By-participant random intercept: participants differ in baseline reading speed.
- By-participant random slope for ambiguity: participants may differ in how much the ambiguity manipulation slows them. This is critical — omitting this slope uses the wrong error term and inflates Type I error. Barr et al. (2013) demonstrate false-positive rates of 20–50% at nominal α = .05 when random slopes are omitted for within-subjects manipulations.
- By-item random intercept: sentences differ in baseline difficulty.
- No by-item random slope for ambiguity: ambiguity does not vary within items (each sentence is fixed as ambiguous or unambiguous), so a by-item random slope is not estimable.

```r
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)

contrasts(d$ambiguity) <- c(-0.5, 0.5)  # sum/effect coding

model <- lmer(RT ~ ambiguity +
                (1 + ambiguity | participant) +
                (1 | item),
              data = d, REML = TRUE)
summary(model)
```

Do not use (1 | participant) alone — that random-intercepts-only model omits the by-participant slope, inflates Type I error, and is almost never defensible for within-subjects manipulations.
